clue.text: Metronome sounds a hundred beats

parts.note: C is a hundred in Roman numerals
to lick a rival is to beat him, and a licking is a thrashing

explanation.surface: A metronome counting out a hundred beats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds' looks like an instruction to listen for a homophone; it is the plural noun, the noises the machine makes. Beating and licking are the same in a schoolyard or a boxing ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A metronome's noise is a dry wooden tick, and clicks is the plural noun for exactly those small sharp sounds.

clue.text: Freer in loose robe, tailor having removed a hoop

indicators.note: Loose things are not fastened down where they were put, so these letters do not stay in the order they are given.
What has been removed is gone before anything else happens, so the letter named next takes no part in what follows.

parts.note: ten letters to work from, one more than the grid has room for
a hoop is a plain ring, which on paper is the letter O — and it is the one taken out

explanation.surface: A tailor working in a loose robe, with a hoop taken out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freer' reads as the comparative of free and is doing a noun's job, which is the hardest kind of definition to spot. The hoop is a letter, not a crinoline.
explanation.definitionFit: A liberator is one who sets people free, so the agent noun 'freer' names the same person by the job rather than by rank.

clue.text: Property's rent rising with gas on top

indicators.note: What rises in a down entry is read from the foot of the column upwards, so those letters arrive the other way round.
Whatever is on top sits above the rest of a down entry, so that piece takes the first squares of the column.

parts.note: to gas is to chat on and on about nothing much
a flat to rent is a flat to let, set down here from the bottom up

explanation.surface: A household's rent going up, with the gas bill on top of that.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface belongs to a tenant's bills, and the wordplay wants the idle-talk sense of gas instead. 'On top' is not scene-setting: it says which piece starts the column.
explanation.definitionFit: Chattels are movable goods — furniture, livestock, anything but the land itself — so a chattel is a single piece of personal property.

clue.text: Perhaps I turned blue

indicators.note: Milk turns and weather turns: to turn is to become something other than you were, which is what these letters do.

parts.note: eight letters to work from, exactly the number the grid wants

explanation.surface: Somebody admitting that they, perhaps, went blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Two short words are the entire fodder, which is why the clue looks as though it has no wordplay in it at all. The colour is named after the gem, not after the cold the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapphire is the deep blue of the gemstone and a colour word in its own right — sapphire skies, sapphire silk.

clue.text: Level unfinished mud pies that aren't crusted over

indicators.note: Something unfinished stops before its end, so the word beside it hands over all but its last letter.
Turned over, a thing lies the opposite way up, so the letters assembled here are read from the far end back.

parts.note: MUD stopping short of its final letter
a tart is an open pie, with no pastry lid baked over the filling

explanation.surface: A child's mud pies, unfinished and left open with no crust over them.
explanation.walkthrough: The pies of the surface are a child's; the pies of the wordplay are the baker's, and an open one is a tart. 'Over' is the only word telling you the assembly is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A stratum is one layer in a stack of rock, or of society, and a layer is a level.

clue.text: Russian who disappeared left in shame

definitions.note: 'Disappeared' is used transitively, the way a regime disappears its critics: the definition names the man who did the disappearing, not one who vanished.

indicators.note: What is in something sits inside it, so the letter named before goes between the letters of the word that follows.

parts.note: a stain on a reputation is a shame attached to it
L is left, as stamped inside a pair of boots

explanation.surface: A Russian who went missing after leaving in disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: Nobody lost Stalin: he is the one who did the disappearing, of rivals and of faces painted out of official photographs. He was Georgian by birth, though the clue counts him Russian.
explanation.definitionFit: Stalin ran the Soviet Union for three decades and had his opponents disappeared — shot, sent to the camps, erased from the record.

clue.text: Quickly list river fish from France

parts.note: R is river on a map
the long thin one, and the crossword's favourite
of and from do the same job: a man of Kent is a man from Kent
F is France on the oval plate stuck to the back of a car

explanation.surface: A river fish brought over from France.
explanation.walkthrough: Four short pieces stack up, and the last two split a word the surface reads as a single phrase. The international plate is worth knowing: F on a car boot means the car is French.
explanation.definitionFit: To reel something off is to rattle through it without pausing — names, dates, excuses — which is listing at speed.

clue.text: Daughter lifts pretty heavy material

indicators.note: Whoever does the lifting stands underneath the load, so in a down entry this letter goes to the foot of the column.

parts.note: twee is pretty in the dainty, faintly embarrassing way
D is daughter on a family tree

explanation.surface: A daughter hauling up a fairly heavy roll of cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty heavy' reads as one phrase meaning fairly heavy, and the split between those two words is where the clue hides. Twee — chintzy, over-dainty — is the sense wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweed is the thick rough wool of jackets and caps, woven heavy enough to keep a Scottish hillside out.

clue.text: Body changes hard for pal raised and housed by religious patriarch

indicators.note: What is raised in a down entry is read from the foot of the column upwards, so those words go in backwards.

parts.note: Moses led the Israelites out of Egypt, and here he opens to take the rest in

indicators.note: To house something is to give it a roof and walls, so the name that follows opens up and takes the rest inside.

parts.note: a pal is a mate, set down from the bottom up
to be for something is to be pro it, also written upwards
H is hard, the grade stamped on a pencil

explanation.surface: Hard changes to a friend's body, brought up and sheltered by a religious patriarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Three pieces go inside Moses, two of them turned round, which is a great deal of instruction for one sentence to hide. 'For' meaning pro is worth learning; setters reach for it constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: A metamorphosis is a change of form so complete the creature is unrecognisable — the caterpillar's, or Gregor Samsa's — so the plural names body changes.

clue.text: Fernando's group led by Jack, a big fat slug

indicators.note: Whoever leads goes at the front, so the letter named here heads the column of letters.

parts.note: J is the jack in a pack of cards
Fernando was the Swedish quartet's biggest-selling single

explanation.surface: The band behind Fernando, fronted by a man called Jack and written off as a big fat slug.
explanation.walkthrough: Jabba the Hutt is the bloated crime lord of Return of the Jedi, so the definition is literal description rather than abuse. 'Fernando's group' names the song's owners, not a man called Fernando.
explanation.definitionFit: Jabba the Hutt is Star Wars' sluglike gangster, vast and immobile on his dais, so the words describe him exactly as drawn.

clue.text: Non-Darwinian fictions only help right-wingers

parts.note: only this much and just this much set the same limit
the call a ship in trouble sends out
the Tories are Britain's Conservative party, the right of its two big ones

explanation.surface: A complaint that invented stories against evolution only serve the political right.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling explains the leopard's spots by storytelling rather than by selection, which is what makes his tales non-Darwinian. 'Help' is a signal flare, not the verb the sentence seems to need.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's Just So Stories account for the camel's hump and the elephant's trunk by tale rather than natural selection, and the phrase now means any such handy invention.

clue.text: Tie up soldiers in empty Pret for work experience

indicators.note: What is in something is held inside it, so these letters are set down between the letters of the emptied word.
An empty thing has nothing in the middle, so the word beside it keeps only its first and last letters.

parts.note: Pret is the British sandwich chain Pret A Manger, here with its middle gone
to lace a boot is to tie it up
an officer's men are his soldiers

explanation.surface: Soldiers tying things up in a deserted branch of Pret.
explanation.walkthrough: A high-street name doing the work of two letters is unusual and worth watching for once you know the chain. 'Tie up' is the shoelace sense, not the hostage one the soldiers invite.
explanation.definitionFit: A placement is the spell in a real workplace that a student does as part of a course — work experience under its formal name.

clue.text: Special hire car from list, hot Merc convertible

indicators.note: Something convertible can be turned into another form, so these letters are free to come out as another.

parts.note: eleven letters to work from, exactly the number the grid wants

explanation.surface: Choosing a hot convertible Merc from a hire company's list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convertible' is a car with a folding roof on the surface and an instruction underneath, which is why the fodder sits so comfortably in the sentence. A Merc is a Mercedes.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretch limo is the lengthened limousine hired out by the hour for weddings and stag nights, so it is a special car for hire.

clue.text: Faint half-way through spinning

indicators.note: A thing spinning comes round to face the other way, so these three letters are read from the end back.

parts.note: the point half-way through anything is its mid point

explanation.surface: Feeling faint half-way through a spin class.
explanation.walkthrough: Three words of gym talk, and only the last of them is an instruction. 'Faint' is the dim of a distant light rather than the swoon the surface has in mind.
explanation.definitionFit: A faint light or a faint memory is a dim one — barely there, hard to make out.

clue.text: People who have moved in crossing line with dogs

indicators.note: To cross a line is to pass through it, so the letter naming one is planted inside the word beside it.

parts.note: the Irish and English gun dogs that freeze when they scent a bird
L is line on a plan

explanation.surface: Newcomers to the district walking their dogs over a boundary line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crossing' has to be read as an instruction about position and not as a picture of dogs on a footpath. The definition is a whole clause doing a plural noun's job, which is what makes it slippery.
explanation.definitionFit: Settlers are the people who have arrived somewhere and made their home there — moved in, on the scale of a whole country.

clue.text: Love reversible zip, right?

indicators.note: A reversible coat works either way round, and so do these two letters — they go in back to front.

parts.note: sweet FA — Fanny Adams — is nothing at all, which is what zip means
a fair decision is a right one

explanation.surface: Someone enthusing about a two-way zip and asking for agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark turns the clue into chat about a jacket. 'Zip' is the American nothing, and sweet Fanny Adams is the British phrase supplying its two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A love affair is shortened in ordinary speech to its second word, so the noun on its own names a romance.

clue.text: Level with secretary about lusts

indicators.note: What goes about a thing is wrapped round it, so the word in front parts and takes the rest inside.

parts.note: a minister's aide is the secretary at his elbow
he lusts after it, he longs for it — the verb in the third person

explanation.surface: Being straight with a secretary about their appetites.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Level with' reads as the idiom for coming clean and means drawing level instead. 'Lusts' is the verb, which is where the S in the middle comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse that comes alongside the leader has drawn level with it, so the preposition says exactly that.

clue.text: Intimidate pig, taking pressure off colleague

indicators.note: The pig is the one doing the taking, so whatever is named next comes out of the pig and not out of anything else.
Taken off means taken away: the letter leaves the word rather than joining onto it.

parts.note: to cow somebody is to frighten them into doing as they are told
a pig is a porker, and it gives up one letter — the next block says which
P is pressure in a physics formula, and it is the letter the porker loses

explanation.surface: Bullying a pig in order to take the pressure off a colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration gives away that the answer opens with a two-letter piece, which narrows the word for intimidating to one candidate. 'Pressure' is a letter here, not a mood.
explanation.definitionFit: A co-worker is someone you work beside — the American office's word for what a British one calls a colleague.

clue.text: Quiet station reduced its capacity

parts.note: the hiss a librarian makes for quiet
a person's station in life is their rank

explanation.surface: A sleepy railway station cutting the number of trains it can take.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Station' is the railway's on the surface and a person's standing underneath, which is the sense that pays. The definition is a whole phrase where one past-tense verb would do.
explanation.definitionFit: Whatever shrank got smaller, and a smaller thing holds less than it held before — its capacity is reduced by the shrinking.

clue.text: Never happy in the highest society

definitions.note: The definition is a noun phrase where the answer is a superlative adjective; 'the' in front of a superlative names the people it describes, as in 'the brave' or 'the good'.

parts.note: no smoking means smoke at no time, which is never
blest is the old short spelling of blessed, and the blessed are the happy ones

explanation.surface: Somebody who is never happy among the grandest people.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a miserable guest at a very good party, and the joining word in the middle carries no letters at all. 'Blest' is the poets' spelling, still sung in hymns.
explanation.definitionFit: The noblest are the families highest in rank, dukes above earls above everyone else, so the superlative names the top of society.

clue.text: Castle housing very old hotel, quaint indeed

indicators.note: A house takes people in and keeps them there, so the word in front opens and holds what follows inside it.

parts.note: a castle is a fort, and this one opens to take the next pieces in
so tired and very tired are the same complaint
O is the standard short form of old
Hotel is H in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A castle with a very old hotel inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quaint indeed' defines and warns at the same time: the word wanted is the archaic one, kept alive now only by mock-medieval speech. Hotel gives H because of the radio alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Forsooth is the old word for indeed, so the definition supplies the meaning and flags the archaism in a single phrase.

clue.text: Cold drink Bond necks? A strong one, for his countrymen

definitions.text: A strong one, for his countrymen

indicators.note: To neck a drink is to send it straight down the throat, so those letters disappear inside the word beside them.

parts.note: Bond is the spy of the films, and he opens up to swallow what follows
C is cold, as marked on a British tap
the sailor's spirit, served from the barrel at noon

explanation.surface: James Bond knocking back a cold drink, and a strong English one at that.
explanation.walkthrough: Bond drinks martinis, so the joke is putting a farmyard cider in his hand instead. 'Necks' is the swallowing verb doing an instruction's work.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrumpy is the rough, cloudy farm cider of England's West Country, far stronger than the bottled kind, and English is what Bond is.

clue.text: Light greeting ICU nurses on the way back

indicators.note: A nurse keeps her patient in her care, so the words in front are holding the letters wanted inside them.
Going back along a road means covering it the other way, so that run of letters is read from its end to its start.

parts.note: six letters in an unbroken row, starting inside the first word and finishing inside the initials

explanation.surface: Saying hello to the intensive-care nurses on the way back.
explanation.walkthrough: The run begins in the middle of a word and ends inside a set of initials, which is a nasty place to hide six letters. 'Light' is the verb, to set alight.
explanation.definitionFit: To light a fire is to ignite it: the two verbs take the same object and name the same act.

clue.text: Smooth snakes shedding skin

indicators.note: A snake sheds what is on the outside of it, so the word beside this loses the letter at each end.

parts.note: a river that snakes coils to and fro across the valley
the outermost letter at each end, the skin of that word, comes away

explanation.surface: Smooth snakes sloughing off their old skins.
explanation.walkthrough: The smooth snake is a real British reptile, rare and protected, so the surface reads as natural history rather than instruction. 'Smooth' is the verb: to oil a hinge is to smooth its action.
explanation.definitionFit: To oil a mechanism is to smooth it, and to oil somebody's path is to smooth that too.

clue.text: Spinner used to turn stumps and bails, perhaps

definitions.text: Spinner used to turn stumps and bails, perhaps

parts.note: read as the slow bowler who puts spin on the ball, and meant as the workshop machine that spins whatever is clamped in it

parts.words: used to turn stumps and bails, perhaps
parts.note: on the surface a bowler beating the wicket; underneath, turning is what a woodworker does to a length of timber, and those two are examples of what comes off it

explanation.surface: A spin bowler forever knocking the stumps and bails over.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket owns every word here and none of it is wordplay. The hinge is 'turn': the bowler turns the ball, the machine turns the wood that stumps and bails are shaped from.
explanation.definitionFit: A lathe spins wood against a chisel to shape it, and cricket stumps and bails are among the turned wooden objects that come off one.

clue.text: Resort's toilet vagrant rogers in

parts.note: bog is the blunt British word for a lavatory

indicators.note: A vagrant has no fixed address and will not stay put, and neither will the letters beside the word.

parts.note: eight letters to work from, and they go in behind the first three

explanation.surface: A vagrant caught having sex in a seaside resort's public lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: Bognor Regis is a seaside town on the Sussex coast, and its name is doing the smutty work the surface asks for. The Regis was granted after George V convalesced there in 1929.
explanation.definitionFit: Bognor Regis is a resort on the south coast, one of the towns the English seaside holiday was built on.

clue.text: Tattoo covering hip, ten bats? Very well

indicators.note: What covers a thing lies over it, so the word in front parts and wraps round the letters that follow.

parts.note: a tattoo is ink under the skin, and this one opens to cover what follows

indicators.note: Bats means barmy, and letters gone barmy will not stay in the order they were handed over in.

parts.note: six letters to work from, sent barmy by the word after them

explanation.surface: A tattoo spreading across a hip with ten bats in it — very well, then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very well' is the healthy sense and not the weary agreement the question mark sets up. The phrase comes from the pink of health, the flush of a well-fed face.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody in the pink is in glowing health, so saying they are in the pink is saying they are very well.

clue.text: Domestic supply mothers must keep at home

definitions.note: The definition is singular and the answer plural in form: the mains are spoken of as one supply — a house is on the mains — but the word never sheds its S.

indicators.note: To keep a thing is to hold on to it rather than let it go, so the mothers close round what they are told to keep.

parts.note: ma is the nursery word for mother, and more than one of them makes mas
somebody at home is in — the answer given at the door

explanation.surface: The supply that mothers have to keep in the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Domestic supply' sounds like groceries and means the electricity, gas and water piped into a house. IN for at home is a crossword staple worth learning early.
explanation.definitionFit: The mains are the public water, gas and electricity supplies feeding a house, which is a domestic supply exactly.

clue.text: Notice couple carrying wide pumpkin in NY?

indicators.note: What is carried is held inside by whatever carries it, so this letter sits within the word in front.

parts.note: to notice something is to see it, and it opens to carry the next letter
W is the cricket scorer's mark for a wide
to couple two things is to tie them together

explanation.surface: Spotting a couple carrying a wide pumpkin through New York.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that pumpkin is one example of the class rather than a synonym: Americans use it as a pet name for somebody dear. 'Couple' is the verb, to join.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweetie and pumpkin are both affectionate names for a loved one, the American term standing in for the homelier British one.

clue.text: Communist pens short anthem with similar sounds

definitions.note: The definition is a phrase where the answer is a past-tense verb: lines that rhymed are lines that ended with similar sounds, so the phrase completes a sentence the verb would.

indicators.note: To pen an animal is to shut it in a pen, so the communist closes round what comes next.
Something short stops before it should, so the word beside it gives up its last letter.

parts.note: a red is a communist, after the colour of the flag
an anthem sung in church is a hymn, here docked of its final letter

explanation.surface: A communist writing a short anthem whose lines chime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' looks like writing and is the farmyard verb, shutting something in. An anthem and a hymn are the same church song, which is where the shortened piece comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Lines that rhymed ended with similar sounds, which is the whole of what rhyming is.
